cards.front: When your body handles food's large molecules, what does it add to take them apart, and what does it remove to build its own?
cards.back: It adds water to take them apart (one water per link broken) and removes water to build its own (one water per link, counted from the free blocks).
cards.quote: Your body takes food's large molecules apart by adding water, one water for each link it breaks

cards.front: In a chain of building blocks, straight or branched, with no rings or cross-links, n blocks are held together by {{c1::n − 1}} links.
cards.quote: The link count fits a chain, straight or branched, with no rings or cross-links: n blocks, n − 1 links.

cards.front: A {{c1::polymer}} is a large molecule of many monomers linked in a chain.
cards.back: Each link is a chemical bond between two blocks.
cards.quote: A polymer is a large molecule of many monomers linked in a chain; each link is a chemical bond between two blocks.

cards.front: A cell joins 10 sugars into one straight chain by dehydration synthesis. Counted from the free blocks, how many waters' worth of atoms are removed?
cards.back: 9. A chain of 10 blocks has 10 − 1 = 9 links, and each link removes one water's worth of atoms.
cards.quote: Use the first film's rule to predict the waters for a chain of 10 sugars.
cards.section: Explore: build big molecules from small blocks

cards.front: A common fat forms from one glycerol and three fatty acids. Counted from the free pieces, how many waters' worth of atoms are removed?
cards.back: 3. The fat's 4 pieces are joined by 3 links, one water per link.
cards.why: A fat is not a chain, but the one-water-per-link rule still holds.
cards.quote: A common fat is not a chain, but its 4 pieces still have 3 links.

cards.front: Starch, proteins, nucleic acids and lipids are all large molecules. Which one is not a polymer, and why?
cards.back: Lipids. A common fat stops at one glycerol and three fatty acids, so it is not a chain of many repeated blocks.
cards.quote: Starch, proteins and nucleic acids are polymers; lipids are not, as step 3 showed.

cards.front: In dehydration synthesis, which atoms leave when two building blocks link, and what do they form?
cards.back: An H from the end of one block and an OH from the end of the next leave the chain. Together they form one water molecule, H2O.
cards.quote: When the link forms, those three atoms leave the chain: one water molecule, H2O.

cards.front: {{c1::Hydrolysis}} ("splitting with water") puts a water molecule back between two blocks, and the link breaks.
cards.back: The H goes to one block and the OH to the other.
cards.quote: Run backward, hydrolysis ("splitting with water") puts a water molecule back: the H goes to one block and the OH to the other, and the link breaks.

cards.front: On the mass scale chemists use for molecules, glucose weighs about 180. Two glucose molecules join to form maltose. Predict maltose's mass and explain why it is not 360.
cards.back: About 342. 2 × 180 = 360, minus about 18 for the one water molecule removed when the link forms.
cards.why: The atoms are not lost; they leave as water.
cards.quote: The atoms are not lost; they leave as water.

cards.front: Digestion breaks a straight starch chain of 6 glucose units completely into free glucose. How many water molecules does hydrolysis add?
cards.back: 5. A chain of 6 blocks has 6 − 1 = 5 links, and hydrolysis adds one water for each link it breaks.
cards.quote: Digestion is different: hydrolysis does add one water for each link it breaks.
cards.section: The real steps in a cell

cards.front: When a cell builds a polymer, does it really release one water molecule at each link?
cards.back: Usually not. Each kind of molecule is built by its own energy-using route, which usually releases other products. The one-water-per-link count describes atoms, not the cell's steps.
cards.quote: The one-water-per-link count describes atoms, not the cell's steps.
cards.section: The real steps in a cell

cards.front: About {{c1::nine}} amino acids, the essential amino acids, must come from food.
cards.quote: About nine, the essential amino acids, must come from food.

cards.front: Your cells can make some amino acids from sugar. Which element must they add that sugar does not have, and where does it come from?
cards.back: Nitrogen. Sugar supplies carbon, hydrogen and oxygen; the nitrogen is moved from other amino acids.
cards.quote: Your cells can make some amino acids from the carbon, hydrogen and oxygen of sugar, adding nitrogen moved from other amino acids.

cards.front: Name the four classes of large molecule and the building blocks of each.
cards.back: Carbohydrates: simple sugars. Proteins: amino acids. Nucleic acids: nucleotides. Lipids: for fats, fatty acids and glycerol (other lipids differ).
cards.quote: Key idea: Carbohydrates, proteins, nucleic acids and lipids each have their own building blocks and their own main jobs.
cards.section: Explain: four classes, four kinds of job

cards.front: A nucleotide is made of a sugar, a {{c1::phosphate group}} and a base containing nitrogen.
cards.back: Nucleotides are the building blocks of nucleic acids such as DNA and RNA.
cards.quote: A nucleotide is a building block made of a sugar, a phosphate group and a base containing nitrogen.
cards.section: Explain: four classes, four kinds of job

cards.front: Fats and phospholipids are both lipids. How do their main jobs differ?
cards.back: Fats: long-term energy storage and insulation. Phospholipids (and cholesterol): building cell membranes.
cards.quote: Not every lipid is a fat: phospholipids and steroids such as cholesterol are lipids too.
cards.section: Explain: four classes, four kinds of job

cards.front: Which elements do all four classes of large molecule share, and what do proteins and nucleic acids add?
cards.back: All are built mostly from carbon, hydrogen and oxygen. Proteins add nitrogen (most also sulfur); nucleic acids add nitrogen and phosphorus.
cards.quote: An amino acid is a small molecule containing nitrogen that is the building block of proteins; most proteins also contain some sulfur.
cards.section: Explain: four classes, four kinds of job

cards.front: Starch gives quick energy and cellulose builds stiff plant walls, yet both are chains of glucose. What does this show about what decides a molecule's job?
cards.back: The blocks alone do not decide the job. The links between the blocks and the shape the chain takes decide it too.
cards.quote: The blocks, the links between them and the shape they take decide the job.

cards.front: Much of the fiber in whole-wheat bread is cellulose. Can your own enzymes digest it, and does anything in your body break it down?
cards.back: Your own enzymes cannot digest fiber. Bacteria in your gut can break down some of it.
cards.quote: Much of the fiber in whole-wheat bread is cellulose and other cell-wall material; bacteria in your gut can break down some of it.

cards.front: One strand of DNA has the bases A, T, G, C in that order. What bases does the matching strand have, and why does this let DNA be copied?
cards.back: T, A, C, G. Bases pair in a fixed way, A with T and G with C, so each strand can guide the copying of the other.
cards.quote: DNA has two strands whose bases pair in a fixed way, A with T and G with C

cards.front: Heat or acid changes the shape of an enzyme's pocket. Predict what happens to the enzyme's work, and why.
cards.back: The enzyme may stop speeding up its reaction, because the molecule it acts on may no longer fit the changed pocket.
cards.quote: The molecule may no longer fit, so the enzyme may stop speeding up its reaction.

cards.front: Phospholipids have a head attracted to water and tails that are not. Predict how many phospholipids arrange between the watery inside and outside of a cell.
cards.back: They form a double layer: heads face the water on each side and tails hide inside, away from water. This double layer is the cell membrane.
cards.why: A lipid mostly does not mix with water; a phospholipid has one end that does attract water.
cards.quote: A lipid is a molecule that mostly does not mix with water, such as a fat or oil.
cards.section: Explain: four classes, four kinds of job

cards.front: Per 100 g, USDA lists whole-wheat bread with 42.71 g carbohydrate, including 6 g fiber. How many grams of carbohydrate are not fiber?
cards.back: 42.71 − 6 = 36.71 g of carbohydrate that is not fiber.
cards.quote: Bread lists 42.71 grams of carbohydrate, including 6 grams of fiber.
cards.section: Elaborate: what is in the sandwich and its neighbors

cards.front: Per 100 g, peanut butter has 51.36 g fat and 22.31 g carbohydrate. Using about 9 kcal per gram for fat and about 4 kcal per gram for carbohydrate, compare the energy in each.
cards.back: Fat: 51.36 × 9 ≈ 462 kcal. Carbohydrate: 22.31 × 4 ≈ 89 kcal. The fat holds about 5 times as much energy.
cards.quote: Using the energy factors, about how much energy is in the fat of 100 grams of peanut butter?
cards.section: Elaborate: what is in the sandwich and its neighbors

cards.front: In the USDA table (bread, turkey breast, peanut butter, apple, whole milk, olive oil), which two foods have the most protein per 100 g, and what does one of them show?
cards.back: Turkey breast (30.13 g) and peanut butter (22.21 g). Peanut butter is a plant food, so protein is not found only in meat.
cards.quote: Which two foods have the most protein per 100 grams? Is one of them a plant food?
cards.section: Elaborate: what is in the sandwich and its neighbors

cards.front: A student says 100 g of raw apple and 100 g of olive oil should give similar energy because both come from plants. Per 100 g, apple has 13.81 g carbohydrate, 0.26 g protein and 0.17 g fat; olive oil has 100 g fat. Estimate both.
cards.back: Olive oil: 100 × 9 ≈ 900 kcal. Apple: 13.81 × 4 + 0.26 × 4 + 0.17 × 9 ≈ 58 kcal, and really a bit less because fiber gives less energy. What the food is made of sets its energy, not whether it comes from a plant.
cards.why: Uses the rounded factors of about 4 kcal per gram for carbohydrate and protein and about 9 kcal per gram for fat.
cards.quote: These are rounded averages, and fiber gives less energy than other carbohydrate, so real values and food labels can be lower.
cards.section: Elaborate: what is in the sandwich and its neighbors

cards.front: Evaluate the claim "fats and carbohydrates are bad for people" using the jobs of each class of large molecule.
cards.back: The lesson's data and job table do not support the claim; each class has needed jobs. Carbohydrates give quick energy and short-term energy storage. Fats give long-term energy storage and insulation, and other lipids build cell membranes.
cards.why: Rests on the lesson's table of main jobs: each class has its own blocks and its own jobs.
cards.quote: Together these molecules run life processes: proteins and lipids build new cells for growth and repair

cards.front: Iodine solution turns blue-black with starch. When testing bread with iodine, why also test water and a known starch sample?
cards.back: Water is the negative control: it should not react. Known starch is the positive control: it should turn blue-black. Together they show the test works, so a color change in the bread comes from the bread.
cards.quote: For each test, use water as a negative control (it should not react) and a known sample as a positive control (it should)

cards.front: Biuret solution turns violet with protein. Per 100 g, USDA lists protein as 12.45 g in whole-wheat bread, 30.13 g in turkey breast and 0.26 g in apple. Predict the biuret results for the three foods.
cards.back: Violet for turkey and for bread, which both have plenty of protein. Little or no violet for the apple, which has very little protein. These are predictions to test, with controls and repeated trials.
cards.quote: Based on the table, you might expect starch in the bread and protein in the turkey and bread.

cards.front: Trace the protein in a bite of turkey to new protein in your own muscle. Name the reaction at each stage and the water at each link.
cards.back: Digestion splits the turkey's proteins into amino acids by hydrolysis, adding one water per link broken. Your cells then join amino acids into their own proteins by dehydration synthesis, which uses energy and, counted from the free blocks, removes one water per link; that count is atom bookkeeping from free blocks, and real cell steps usually release other products.
cards.why: Combines the take-apart and build-again rules from the start of the lesson.
cards.quote: digestion splits its large molecules into small pieces, such as sugars, amino acids, fatty acids and the parts of nucleotides
